prompt: What is an adiabatic process?

choices.text: One in which no energy is transferred as heat
One in which the temperature stays constant
choices.why: Constant temperature defines an isothermal process. In an adiabatic process q = 0, and the temperature is free to change.

choices.text: One in which the volume stays constant
choices.why: Constant volume defines an isochoric process, where no volume work is done. An adiabatic process is one with no heat transfer, q = 0.

choices.text: One in which no work is done on or by the system
choices.why: An adiabatic gas can still do work, for example by pushing a piston out. What is zero is the heat: δq = 0.

explanation: In an adiabatic process no energy crosses the boundary as heat, so δq = 0 at every step. Work can still be done, and the temperature can change.

prompt: The section takes the word adiabatic apart: a- means not, dia means through, and bat- comes from a Greek verb for walking. What is it that cannot walk through the wall?

choices.text: Energy as heat
The gas molecules
choices.why: The cylinder walls keep the molecules in for any process. The word says that heat cannot pass through the wall.

choices.text: Energy as work
choices.why: An adiabatic gas can still do work through the moving piston. It is heat that cannot get through the wall.

choices.text: Changes in temperature
choices.why: The temperature of an adiabatic gas can and does change. The word refers to heat, which cannot pass through the wall.

explanation: A-dia-bat means not-through-walking. In an adiabatic process the wall, styrofoam in the section's example, keeps heat from walking through, so q = 0.

prompt: How does the section suggest making sure that no heat can enter a gas cylinder as the gas expands?

choices.text: Wrap the cylinder in an insulator such as styrofoam
Keep the cylinder in a large bath at fixed temperature
choices.why: A bath at fixed temperature exchanges heat with the gas to hold T constant, which gives an isothermal process. Insulation is what stops the heat.

choices.text: Peg the piston so that the volume cannot change
choices.why: Fixing the volume stops the gas from doing work, not heat from flowing. To stop heat, the cylinder is insulated.

choices.text: Pull the piston out as fast as possible
choices.why: The section keeps the expansion slow and reversible. Heat is kept out by insulating the cylinder, for instance with styrofoam.

explanation: The section puts the cylinder in styrofoam, an insulator, so that no heat can enter. The piston can still be pulled out slowly, so the expansion is both adiabatic and reversible.

prompt: Can an expansion be adiabatic and reversible at the same time?

choices.text: Yes, if the insulated piston is pulled out slowly
No, an adiabatic process is always irreversible
choices.why: Adiabatic only means that no heat flows. The section's insulated cylinder can still be expanded slowly, which keeps the path reversible.

choices.text: Only if the gas is kept at constant temperature
choices.why: A reversible adiabatic expansion does not keep T constant. It only needs an insulated cylinder and a slow pull on the piston.

choices.text: Only if the gas does no work during the expansion
choices.why: A reversible adiabatic expansion does work, w_rev, on the surroundings. It needs insulation and a slow pull, not zero work.

explanation: Adiabatic (no heat) and reversible (forces balanced at every step) are separate conditions. The section's insulated cylinder with a slowly pulled piston meets both.

prompt: In an adiabatic process δq = 0. What does the first law, dU = δq + δw, then say?

choices.text: dU = δw, so the whole change in U is work
dU = δq, so the whole change in U is heat
choices.why: δq is the term that is zero here. With no heat, only the work is left: dU = δw.

choices.text: dU = 0, so U cannot change
choices.why: U stays the same only if the work is also zero. In an adiabatic expansion the gas does work, so U falls by that amount.

choices.text: dU = −δw, so U rises when the gas does work
choices.why: The sign is wrong: dU = δw. Work done by the gas is negative, so U falls when the gas does work.

explanation: With δq = 0, the first law leaves dU = δw, and for a whole process ΔU = w. Any energy change of the system comes in or goes out as work.

prompt: In a reversible adiabatic expansion, the gas does work on its surroundings, yet no heat enters. Where does the energy for this work come from?

choices.text: The internal energy of the gas itself
Heat that slowly leaks in through the walls
choices.why: In an adiabatic process no heat gets in at all. The work can only be paid for out of the gas's internal energy.

choices.text: Work that the surroundings do on the gas
choices.why: In an expansion the gas does work on the surroundings, not the other way around. The energy comes from the gas's internal energy.

choices.text: Nowhere; the expansion makes new energy
choices.why: Energy is conserved and cannot be created. With q = 0, the work must come out of the internal energy, so U falls.

explanation: With no heat coming in, the only source of the energy is the gas itself. So dU = δw_rev: U falls by exactly the work the gas does.

prompt: A reversible isothermal expansion and a reversible adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas each have one quantity equal to zero. Which is it for each?

choices.text: ΔU = 0 for the isothermal one, q = 0 for the adiabatic one
q = 0 for the isothermal one, ΔU = 0 for the adiabatic one
choices.why: This swaps them. Heat flows in during an isothermal expansion, and U falls in an adiabatic one.

choices.text: w = 0 for the isothermal one, q = 0 for the adiabatic one
choices.why: An isothermal expansion does work, w = −nRT ln(V_2/V_1). What vanishes is ΔU, because U of an ideal gas depends only on T.

choices.text: ΔU = 0 for the isothermal one, w = 0 for the adiabatic one
choices.why: An adiabatic expansion does work, paid for out of U. What vanishes is the heat, q = 0.

explanation: In the isothermal case T is fixed, and U of an ideal gas depends only on T, so ΔU = 0 and w_rev = −q_rev. In the adiabatic case the insulation makes q = 0, so ΔU = w.

prompt: For a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas (V_2 > V_1), q_rev = nRT ln(V_2/V_1). What does the sign of q_rev tell us?

choices.text: Heat has to flow into the gas to keep T constant
Heat flows out of the gas as it expands
choices.why: Since V_2 > V_1, ln(V_2/V_1) is positive, so q_rev > 0. Heat flows in to make up for the work the gas does.

choices.text: No heat flows, because the temperature is fixed
choices.why: Constant temperature does not mean zero heat. Heat must flow in so that ΔU = q_rev + w_rev stays zero while the gas does work.

choices.text: The gas warms up as it expands
choices.why: The temperature is held fixed in an isothermal process. The positive q_rev is heat taken in to balance the work done by the gas.

explanation: With V_2 > V_1, ln(V_2/V_1) > 0, so q_rev is positive: you, or the environment, must put heat into the gas. It exactly balances the work the gas does, keeping ΔU = 0.

prompt: 1.00 mol of an ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at 400 K from 2.0 L to 6.0 L. Since ΔU = 0, the heat absorbed is q_rev = nRT ln(V_2/V_1). Using R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and ln 3 = 1.099, what is q_rev, in J?
explanation: q_rev = (1.00 mol)(8.314 J/(mol·K))(400 K)(1.099) = 3655 J. It is positive, so heat flows into the gas, and w_rev = −q_rev = −3655 J.

prompt: An ideal gas is compressed reversibly and isothermally, and 1.50 kJ of work is done on it (w_rev = +1.50 kJ). Since ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas at constant T, what is q_rev, in kJ? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: ΔU = w_rev + q_rev = 0, so q_rev = −w_rev = −1.50 kJ. The negative sign means that 1.50 kJ of heat flows out of the gas.

prompt: A gas in a well-insulated cylinder is compressed, and the surroundings do 640 J of work on it. Since no heat crosses the insulation, what is ΔU of the gas, in J?
explanation: The process is adiabatic, so q = 0 and ΔU = q + w = 0 + 640 J = 640 J. All the work done on the gas is stored as internal energy.

prompt: 1.00 mol of a monatomic ideal gas, for which U = (3/2)nRT, cools from 320 K to 240 K in a reversible adiabatic expansion. Using R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), what is the work w done on the gas, in J?
explanation: ΔU = (3/2)nR ΔT = (3/2)(1.00 mol)(8.314 J/(mol·K))(−80 K) = −998 J. With q = 0, w = ΔU = −998 J: the gas does 998 J of work on its surroundings.

prompt: To go from (P_1, V_1, T_1) to (P_2, V_2, T_1), the section compares the reversible isothermal expansion A with a two-step path B + C. What are steps B and C?

choices.text: A reversible adiabatic expansion, then heating at constant volume
A reversible isothermal expansion, then cooling at constant volume
choices.why: The isothermal expansion is path A itself. B is the adiabatic expansion, and C is heating at constant volume to bring T back up to T_1.

choices.text: Heating at constant volume, then a reversible adiabatic expansion
choices.why: The order is the other way round. The gas first expands adiabatically along B, cooling to T_2, and is then warmed at constant volume along C.

choices.text: An adiabatic compression, then heating at constant pressure
choices.why: The gas has to end at the larger volume V_2. B is an adiabatic expansion, and C is heating at constant volume.

explanation: Path B is a reversible adiabatic expansion from V_1 to V_2, during which the gas cools to T_2. Path C then warms it at constant volume (isochorically) back to T_1.

prompt: Why is the constant-volume heating C needed after the adiabatic expansion B?

choices.text: The gas cooled along B and must be warmed back to T_1
The gas warmed along B and must be cooled back to T_1
choices.why: The gas does work along B with no heat coming in, so U and T fall. C adds heat to raise T back to T_1.

choices.text: The volume must still be raised from V_1 to V_2
choices.why: The adiabatic expansion B already takes the volume to V_2, and C keeps it there. C is needed to restore the temperature.

choices.text: Step B does no work, so C must supply it
choices.why: Step B does work, while C, at constant volume, does none. C adds heat to bring the cooled gas back to T_1.

explanation: Along the adiabat B, the temperature drops from T_1 to T_2. The isochoric heating C then warms the gas back to T_1, so that B + C ends in the same state as the isotherm A.

prompt: Why must ΔU for the two-step path B + C be the same as ΔU for the isothermal path A?

choices.text: U is a state function, and the end points are the same
Both paths are reversible, so all their energies match
choices.why: Being reversible does not make q or w match; w_A and w_B differ. ΔU matches because U is a state function and the end points are shared.

choices.text: Both paths take in the same amount of heat
choices.why: The heats differ: q_A along the isotherm, q_C along step C. ΔU matches because U depends only on the end states.

choices.text: Both paths do the same amount of work
choices.why: The section shows that w_A and w_B are not equal. ΔU is equal because U is a state function.

explanation: U is a state function, so ΔU depends only on the initial and final states, which paths A and B + C share. The heat and work along the two paths can still differ.

prompt: For an ideal gas, path A and path B + C both have ΔU_tot = 0. Why is it zero rather than some other value?

choices.text: Both ends are at T_1, and U depends only on T
No heat flows along either of the two paths
choices.why: Heat flows along A and along C. ΔU is zero because the start and end are at the same temperature, and U of an ideal gas depends only on T.

choices.text: The volume is the same at the start and the end
choices.why: The volume grows from V_1 to V_2. ΔU = 0 because the temperature is T_1 at both ends.

choices.text: The pressure is the same at the start and the end
choices.why: The pressure falls from P_1 to P_2. What the end points share is the temperature T_1, and U of an ideal gas depends only on T.

explanation: For an ideal gas, U depends only on T; for a monatomic one, U = (3/2)nRT. Both paths start and end at T_1, so ΔU_tot = 0 for each.

prompt: For path B + C the section writes 0 = q_B + w_B + q_C + w_C. Which two terms are zero?

choices.text: q_B and w_C
w_B and q_C
choices.why: These are the terms that remain and cancel each other. q_B is zero because B is adiabatic, and w_C is zero because C is at constant volume.

choices.text: q_B and q_C
choices.why: q_B is zero, but heat is added along C to warm the gas. The other zero is w_C, since no volume work is done at constant volume.

choices.text: w_B and w_C
choices.why: w_C is zero, but the gas does work along B as it expands. The other zero is q_B, since B is adiabatic.

explanation: B is an adiabat, so q_B = 0, and C is an isochore, so w_C = 0. That leaves 0 = w_B + q_C, or w_B = −q_C.

prompt: In the section's path B + C, the constant-volume heating C adds q_C = +1.80 kJ of heat. Using 0 = q_B + w_B + q_C + w_C for the whole path, what is the work w_B done on the gas along the adiabat B, in kJ? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: q_B = 0 on the adiabat and w_C = 0 at constant volume, so w_B = −q_C = −1.80 kJ. The gas does 1.80 kJ of work as it expands along B.

prompt: The section finds that the work w_A along the isotherm differs from the work w_B along the adiabat, although both paths are reversible. What does this show?

choices.text: Work is a path function, even on reversible paths
One of the two paths must really be irreversible
choices.why: Both paths are reversible. Work simply depends on which path is followed, reversible or not.

choices.text: U is not a state function after all
choices.why: ΔU is the same (zero) for both paths, as a state function's change must be. It is w, a path function, that differs.

choices.text: The first law fails for adiabatic processes
choices.why: The first law holds along both paths: ΔU = q + w = 0 in each case. The heat and work just split differently.

explanation: Paths A and B + C share their end points and their ΔU, yet w_A ≠ w_B. Even when every step is reversible, work depends on the path.

prompt: Along the adiabat B, the section writes a straight d instead of δ for the work. Why is that allowed there?

choices.text: With δq = 0, the work equals dU
The work along an adiabat is always zero
choices.why: The gas does work along the adiabat. The straight d is allowed because, with δq = 0, that work is the whole of dU.

choices.text: The adiabat is an irreversible path
choices.why: Path B is reversible. The d is allowed because the work is the only contribution to dU when no heat flows.

choices.text: The volume does not change along the adiabat
choices.why: The volume grows from V_1 to V_2 along B. The d is allowed because with δq = 0 the work equals the state-function change dU.

explanation: Along an adiabat δq = 0, so dU = δw: the work is the only contribution to the change in the state function U. That is why the section can write it with a straight d.
